title: Hashing, complements, and canonical keys

transfer.prompt: A stream contains customer IDs and amounts. Return how many earlier purchases by the same customer make a pair totaling T with the current purchase. Negative amounts and duplicates are allowed.
hints: Which fields must be part of a key?
What information is lost if you store only one earlier index?
transfer.solution: Maintain customer → amount → long frequency. For each record, add the count of T-currentAmount in that customer bucket, then increment currentAmount. Query before insert excludes self-pairing. Expected O(n) time and O(n) space; count pairs in long and use overflow-aware arithmetic if amounts span all long values.

title: Two pointers and safe elimination

transfer.prompt: A sorted list of sensor readings must be split into as many disjoint pairs as possible, each with sum at most a limit. Every unpaired reading is allowed. Return the maximum pair count.
hints: Consider the largest remaining reading.
If it cannot fit with the smallest, can it fit with anyone?
transfer.solution: Use opposite endpoints. If smallest+largest exceeds the limit, discard the largest as unpairable. Otherwise pair them and advance both. An exchange argument shows an optimum can use this pair: if each endpoint was paired elsewhere, re-pair their partners, whose sum is no greater than the original feasible cross-sum. O(n) time and O(1) space; sortedness is required.

title: Sliding windows: expand, repair, and count

transfer.prompt: In a stream of device events, find the longest contiguous period involving at most three device IDs, where each ID may appear no more than twice.
hints: There are two independent reasons a window becomes invalid.
Can removing the oldest event ever make either constraint worse?
transfer.solution: Maintain per-ID frequencies, number of distinct IDs, and number of IDs with frequency above two. Add right; shrink left while distinct>3 or overfull>0. Both constraints improve or stay unchanged under deletion, so the earliest valid left yields the longest valid ending interval. Expected O(n) time and O(1) bounded active state, plus a transient extra ID.

title: Prefix sums, balance, and range counting

transfer.prompt: Given daily integer profit, return the longest nonempty period whose total profit is divisible by a positive integer m. Loss days are allowed.
hints: What relation must the two boundary prefixes satisfy?
For the longest period, which occurrence of each residue should survive?
transfer.solution: Normalize cumulative residues modulo m. Seed residue 0 at boundary index 0. At each boundary r, if its residue first appeared at l, r-l is a divisible period; retain only the earliest l and maximize the distance. Expected O(n) time and O(min(n,m)) space. Unlike counting, frequencies are unnecessary.

title: Binary search on positions, structure, and answers

transfer.prompt: Jobs arrive in fixed order. A worker processes one contiguous batch per day. Each nonempty day also consumes a fixed setup cost c from its capacity. Find the smallest daily capacity needed to finish within D days.
hints: Can the setup cost be separated from the variable workload limit?
What happens to feasibility when capacity grows?
transfer.solution: For nonnegative job workloads and c>=0, any nonempty day at capacity C can process at most C-c workload. Greedily pack in order using this effective capacity; search from maxJob+c to sumJobs+c. Larger C cannot increase needed days, so first-feasible binary search works in O(n log(sumJobs+1)) time and O(1) auxiliary space. Empty input requires no setup and returns zero; use overflow-aware long bounds.

title: Sorting, intervals, scheduling, and sweep lines

transfer.prompt: A service receives temporary capacity grants [start,end,units]. Find the earliest time at which active capacity reaches at least a target, using half-open time intervals.
hints: Which two events does each grant create?
What does an end and start at the same coordinate mean for the observed capacity?
transfer.solution: Create +units at start and -units at end; sort by coordinate and sum all deltas at equal coordinates before checking the threshold. The aggregate is capacity on the following time span. Return the first coordinate meeting the target, or absence. O(n log n) time, O(n) events; use long for units totals. If target<=0 and time is unbounded, "earliest" needs an explicit domain start.

title: Linked lists: preserve the path while changing links

transfer.prompt: A conveyor log is a chain of event objects. Reverse each consecutive block whose size is specified by the next entry in a size array; leave an incomplete final block untouched. Preserve every event identity. Derive an in-place algorithm.
hints: A block size changes how far you probe, not the reversal primitive.
Keep a predecessor and validate the entire block before changing edges.
transfer.solution: Use a dummy and a boundary predecessor. For each positive block size, probe that many nodes; if absent, stop. Save the successor, reverse until that successor, reconnect the predecessor, advance to the old first node. Across processed blocks, each node is scanned at most twice: O(n+s) time for n reachable nodes and s sizes examined, O(1) auxiliary space. Reject nonpositive sizes before mutating if all-or-nothing validation is required.

title: Stacks, monotonic frontiers, and deques

transfer.prompt: A monitoring service receives timestamped scores in increasing timestamp order. After each event, report the maximum score among events no more than 60 seconds old. Several events can share a timestamp. Design the state.
hints: Expiration uses timestamps rather than a fixed count.
A newer score at least as large can replace an older score.
transfer.solution: Keep a deque of (timestamp,sequence,score). Remove front records with timestamp<now-60, remove back records with score≤newScore, then append the event. Front is the maximum. Each event enters and leaves at most once: amortized O(1) processing and O(w) space for events in the active time span. Specify inclusive age and require nondecreasing input time; out-of-order arrivals break the expiration and dominance proof.

title: Trees: decide what crosses each parent-child boundary

transfer.prompt: In a company hierarchy, each employee has an integer benefit. Select a nonempty chain of directly connected employees, possibly climbing then descending once, to maximize total benefit. A manager may have many direct reports. Derive the returned state.
hints: A simple chain can use at most two child branches at its highest manager.
Only one branch can be exposed to a manager above.
transfer.solution: Postorder each employee, retain the two largest positive child downward gains, update best with employee benefit plus both, return employee benefit plus the largest. This generalizes the binary-tree path proof to arbitrary degree. O(n) time/O(h) stack when scanning each reporting edge once; use Long and preserve an all-negative answer.

title: Heaps: keep the next winner and forget full order

transfer.prompt: A service reads many sorted files of timestamps and must publish only the first 1000 events globally, preserving source order for equal timestamps. Design the candidate state without loading all files.
hints: Only one unread head per file can win next.
A deterministic tie rule can include file index and per-file sequence.
transfer.solution: Maintain a min-heap of (timestamp,fileId,sequence,event) for one current head per nonempty file. Pop, publish, and read the next record from that file until 1000 events or exhaustion. O(k+1000 log(k+1)) heap work after seeding k files and O(k) memory, excluding output and I/O buffers. The tie key must match the exact meaning of source order; no global stable order exists across different files unless specified.

title: Backtracking: enumerate choices with a reversible state

transfer.prompt: Generate all meal plans of exactly d days using dishes with positive costs. Total cost must equal budget, no two adjacent days may use the same dish, and order across days matters. Derive the search state and safe pruning.
hints: Day order matters, so increasing dish indices would discard valid plans.
Track remaining budget and the previous dish identity.
transfer.solution: State is day,remainingBudget,previousDish,path. Try every dish except previous; subtract its positive cost, recurse, and undo. At day d accept only zero remainder. Prune if remainder is below remainingDays×minimumCost or above remainingDays×maximumCost; these relaxed bounds are safe even though adjacency may make them unattainable. O(m^d·d) worst-case including output for m dishes, O(d) auxiliary state. Use Long for cost bounds and budget; additional memoization helps counting or feasibility, but enumeration still needs distinct paths.

title: Tries: share prefixes and prune impossible continuations

transfer.prompt: A router receives URL paths split into segments. Rules contain literal segments or a wildcard matching exactly one segment. Return whether any complete rule matches a request path; a rule ending early must not match longer paths. Design the index and search.
hints: Treat whole segments as symbols rather than individual characters.
A terminal marker still distinguishes a complete rule from a prefix.
transfer.solution: Build a trie with a map of literal segment children and a separate wildcard child. Query state is node and request-segment index; try the matching literal and wildcard edge, and accept only at the final index on a terminal node. O(V) visited compatible nodes and O(depth) stack, potentially branching per segment. Normalize/parse URLs before indexing under an explicit policy; prefix sharing and terminal logic are unchanged by the new alphabet.

title: Graphs: reachability and shortest unweighted paths

transfer.prompt: Several charging stations are placed in an unweighted warehouse grid with blocked cells. For every open cell, return the minimum walking steps to any station, or -1 if unreachable.
hints: Running one independent search per cell repeats almost all work.
Reverse the perspective: start every station at distance zero.
transfer.solution: Initialize all station cells as discovered with distance 0 in one queue. BFS through legal open neighbors and assign distance parent+1 on first discovery. Queue layering proves minimum distance from the whole starting set. O(R*C) time and space; absent stations leave all distances -1.

title: Dependency order and dynamic connectivity

transfer.prompt: A build tool receives directed package prerequisites and undirected cable additions between build workers. It needs a feasible package build order and whether two workers currently communicate. Choose state and algorithms for each query.
hints: An arrow imposes order; a cable expresses symmetric reachability.
Ask whether your state needs readiness counts or equivalence classes.
transfer.solution: Use directed adjacency and indegrees with Kahn for package order, O(P+D) time/space for P packages and D dependency edges. Use DSU for workers: union on cable additions and compare find roots for connectivity; O((W+Q) alpha(W)) total for initialization plus Q operations, O(W) space. DSU cannot answer directed prerequisite feasibility or show the actual cable path.

title: Shortest paths: matching the frontier to edge costs

transfer.prompt: A robot moves in a warehouse. Entering a free aisle costs 0 energy and entering a charging-door cell costs 1 energy. Find the smallest energy from the entrance to exit; there is no limit on moves. Then explain what changes if the robot can open at most two doors but must minimize walking steps.
hints: Energy and move count are different objectives.
For the second version, how does remaining door budget affect legal future moves?
transfer.solution: For minimum energy with 0/1 entry costs, use zero-one BFS, front-pushing zero-cost improvements and back-pushing one-cost improvements: O(R*C) time/space. For minimum steps under two doors, use ordinary BFS over (r,c,doorsUsed) with at most 3*R*C states. The complete state distinguishes arrivals with different remaining capabilities. A single distance per cell would discard useful routes.

title: Greedy choices and exchange arguments

transfer.prompt: A camera battery can cover any interval of time up to its charge length. Given start/end times for shows on one camera, choose the largest number of complete nonoverlapping shows. Touching endpoints are allowed. Now each show has a different revenue: does the same method maximize revenue?
hints: Ignore revenue first. Compare two possible first shows by their end times.
Try one long high-revenue show versus two short low-revenue shows.
transfer.solution: For count, sort by ending time and greedily accept compatible shows: exchange any optimal first show with the earliest-finishing one. O(n log n) time. Revenue breaks the count-preserving exchange; sort by end, find each compatible predecessor by binary search and use dp[i]=max(dp[i−1],value[i]+dp[p(i)]), O(n log n) time and O(n) space.

title: Linear dynamic programming: decisions, states, and dependencies

transfer.prompt: A row of machines offers integer rewards. If you activate machine i, the next two machines must remain inactive. Find the maximum reward, allowing no activation.
hints: Define the answer for the first i machines.
How far back is the last prefix that can coexist with taking the current machine?
transfer.solution: Let dp[i] be the optimum for the first i machines, with dp[0]=0 and out-of-range negative prefixes treated as zero. For current machine i-1, skip gives dp[i-1], take gives reward[i-1]+dp[max(0,i-3)]. Thus dp[i]=max of these choices. O(n) time and O(n) table, compressible to three prior states in O(1) space; keep the table for reconstruction.

title: Dynamic programming on grids and strings

transfer.prompt: A migration tool converts a sequence of schema tokens into another using insert, delete or rename, each with a given nonnegative fixed cost. Derive the cheapest conversion. Then suppose renaming a token costs less if the previous action was also a rename: what changes?
hints: Define the answer for every pair of consumed token-prefix lengths.
Does a prefix pair alone determine the future cost after the discount rule is added?
transfer.solution: With fixed context-free costs, use edit-distance DP: min(delete cost+above, insert cost+left, rename/match cost+diagonal). Base rows/columns are accumulated insertion/deletion costs. O(mn) time and O(n) score-only space. A previous-action discount requires an additional state for the last action type, or another sufficient summary of discount eligibility. The old two-dimensional state merges histories with different future costs and is no longer sufficient.

title: Range queries: precompute reusable pieces, then update only dependencies

transfer.prompt: A live leaderboard assigns each known player a score. Support point score replacement and ask for the maximum score among player IDs in an interval. Later product asks for the number of players whose score is below a threshold. Explain whether the same index answers both efficiently.
hints: The first query orders players by ID. The second orders them by score.
A segment maximum loses the distribution below its maximum.
transfer.solution: A segment tree indexed by player ID supports replacement and interval maximum in O(log n), storing one maximum per node. It cannot answer score-threshold counts from those maxima alone because many distributions share the same maximum. For a global threshold count with known score coordinates, maintain a separate frequency Fenwick tree over compressed scores, decrementing the old rank and incrementing the new rank on replacement. If new scores arrive outside known coordinates, use an order-statistic balanced tree or rebuild compression; for both an ID interval and score threshold, a two-dimensional data structure is required.

title: Bit manipulation and state compression

transfer.prompt: A workshop has n <= 15 jobs and n workers. cost[i][j] is the fee for worker j doing job i. Every worker can do exactly one job. Find the minimum total fee without enumerating all n! assignments. Fees are nonnegative and totals fit Long.
hints: Process jobs in a fixed order; what information determines which workers remain available?
Represent that chosen set with a mask and derive the next job index from its number of set bits.
transfer.solution: Let dp[mask] be the minimum fee for assigning the first popcount(mask) jobs to exactly the workers in mask. Start dp[0]=0. For every unused worker j, relax dp[mask | (1<<j)] with dp[mask]+cost[popcount(mask)][j]. Future choices depend only on this set, so discard more expensive histories. Return dp[(1<<n)-1]. O(n*2^n) time, O(2^n) space, with no input mutation. This is the final XOR assignment problem with a general cost matrix.
